course_description:
This course highlights key problems of both physical and human dimensions of global change and analyses their origins, patterns and prognoses for the future. Learning is accomplished by lectures, readings and participation in class debates on major issues. Extensive use of contemporary sources (print and television current affairs, news reports and commentaries etc) can be anticipated.

This course actively examines the knowledge bases and tools used to investigate global changes and for developing and applying approaches to understand, and address these from local to global scales. In doing so, the physical, biological, social, economic, cultural and human dimensions of global change processes will be explored and integrated. The course examines how we understand global changes, and uses this to develop potential actions for sustainable societies from local to global scales.ﾠStudents are exposed to key topics associated with global changes and will be expected to gain an appreciation of global change issues, and how we can can take actions in professional and personal contexts to address these. The course is based around weekly in-person lecture-briefs and tutorial activities, with a focus on developing and applying constructive critical discussions, collaborations and communication skills.

course_aims:
The aim of this course is to provide a detailed overview to students of issues associated with global change, particularly different knowledge systems, and geo-spatial tools used to develop and communicate an understanding of local to global scale changes, especially the linked human and physical dimensions of global change processes.

This aim will be achieved through buildingﾠunderstanding through reading, discussions and reflections on the content of course material and research/knowledge synthesis achieved in compilation of the assignments.

learning_outcomes.description: Define and explain the term global change and discuss related physical, social, cultural, economic and environmental problems and prospects.
Examine the spatial tools that are utilized in the investigation of global change.
Analyse and explain the physical dimensions associated with global change processes.
Analyse and explain the socio-cultural dimensions associated with global change processes.
Demonstrate insight into the future prospects of global change issues.
Employ verbal and written communication skills effectively to articulate your knowledge.
Reflect on your own learning experiences within the course.
Discuss research findings in the area of global change.

assessment_details.title: Recorded Presentation on National to Local Scale Adaptation to Global Change
assessment_details.other_conditions: Student specific, Time limited. See the conditions definitions
assessment_details.task_description: This project is an investigation into a "Global Change and Solution" to set out how you will build a detailed understanding of it, and how it is being addressed at local, nation-state or global scales. The primary objectives of this assessment are: To build a detailed understanding and preliminary assessment of one type of "global change", including its known causes/drivers, impacts and approaches taken to reduce negative impacts of this change at local scales at a location in Australia Task: Integrate the practical skills and knowledge of global change you have developed in the course this assessment item requires you to prepare a recorded presentation providing a 5-minute long "project briefing" video. This is an individual task. Refer to Assessment Section of the course Blackboard page, for detailed instructions, submission template and grading criteria In the Briefing Video you outline to an audience from the general public, a specific type of global change, along with examples of its impacts and management at a local scale in Australia, and a brief assessment of how effective its management has been. Your aim is to use the brief to convince the audience that: - the global change dimension you assess is established based on credible scientific evidence; - the local scale impacts of the global change dimension you assess are identifiable and can be attributed to global scale changes; - specific management actions have been taken by a form of government or community group to adapt to, and/or mitigate the local scale impacts; and - that you have evidence from a critical assessment of the management measures if they are reducing impacts and risk from the global scale change. All instructions for completing and submitting this assessment item, including an example presentation, are on the course Blackboard site. Media to Use: Your recording can be compiled using PowerPoint, Prezi, or any other software. The presentation will need to be based on material covered during the semester, along with significant amount of background research in peer-reviewed literature. The presentation will need to be based primarily on relevant graphic (images, maps, graphs, photos, diagrams), with limited use of detailed text, e.g. less than 30% of each slide. Options for recording your presentation – this must include you speaking to camera and your visuals: a) PowerPoints Record function b) Zoom recording c) Open source or proprietary video recording and editing software e.g. https://obsproject.com/ or other options The submitted materia l, in a single word or PDF document, though the course Blackboard site submission link should include the following: - Title page, including your “topic”, course name, student number - Contents listing - Link to an accessible site where you have uploaded your video, e.g. YouTube - Dot-point outline of your presentation, e.g. headings and dot points - Reference list including all materials used to generate the content and presentation The recording is not to be sped up to meet the 5-minute limit - modified videos will be deducted grades for this. Permissible Use of Generative AI Content in Assessment Item - This Assessment tasks allows use of AI to research and design the presentation. AI cannot be used to deliver the presentation. All uses of AI tools must be fully documented and acknowledged to identify which parts of the assessment were produced using AI tools. This assessment task evaluates students' abilities, skills and knowledge, ideally without the aid of Artificial Intelligence (AI). Students are advised that the use of AI technologies beyond the limits set here, is strictly prohibited and may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct. Some advice: Refer to the Student Support website and the Graphic Presentation tutorial for information on the presentation of your assessment item. Please consult Student Services website ( www.uq.edu.au/student ) for workshops and general advice on essay writing. The Library also offers workshops in the use of EndNote bibliographic referencing software. Read full task description Hide full task description

learning_activities.topic: Week 1: Introduction: Global Changes - Local to Global Solutions Introduction: Global Changes - Local to Global Solutions, course profile discussion, introductory concepts, core skill building (reflective writing)

Week 2: Global Change and National "Security/Securities": Which one and Why ? Global Change and National "Security/Securities": Which one and Why ? Approaches for sustainable environments and societies: Review and discussion of approaches and ways forwards with - conservation, technology, natural capital - ecosystem services, traditional knowledge and practices.

Week 3: How to measure global scale changes - Earth System Sciences - Biophysical + Social Overview of the disciplines and techniques used to make measurements at global scales, and subsequent measurement, monitoring and modelling of biophysical, social, cultural and economic changes at global scales.

Week 4: Global Climate Change - Collective Human Impacts, Adaptation and Mitigation? Integrative assessment of the evidence bases for global scale climate changes and the linkages between human activities and measured changes, along with select examples of adaptation and mitigation programs from local to national and global scales.

Week 5: How Natural Catastrophic Events Create Global Change Exploration of a range of natural catastrophic events, the nature of the events and the scales of their impacts on biophysical processes globally and human activities at local scales.

Week 6: The Anthropocene: How Human Beings Changed the World The Anthropocene: How Human Beings Changed the World - What are our next steps ?This lecture examines a newly defined geological period - The Anthropocene

Week 7: Spaceship Earth - Human Population Dynamics: Local to Global Scale Dynamics What is the population of the planet ? How quickly is it changing and how is it changing? What are the processes driving population changes within and between cities and countries, and how are these driven by global scale changes?

Week 8: - Sustainable Cities ? What does the future of human settlements look like, in Australia and in a range of areas around the planet ? What is driving these changes and what type of society will these changes produce ?

Week 9: Circular Bioeconomy and Industrial Ecology: Pathways to Food and Water Security in a Changing World Are food and water security our primary local and national security concerns ? How do we use and improve our capabilities for recycling and efficient production systems, to minimise waste in many forms, and ensure food and water supply meets demands?

Week 10: - Global Biodiversity - Where is it going ? Global Biodiversity: This session examines elements of global biodiversity and whether we are heading into the sixth mass extinction event in Earth's history.

Week 11: Understanding and Actions: Environmental Sociology and Political Sciences What drives how individuals, communities and societies to make decisions and act, especially in relation to addressing local scale impacts of global changes, and how this is recognised and addressed in political and government systems.

Week 12: Indigenous experiences and understanding of global changes Exploration of several forms of indigenous knowledge development and communication, and their application to understanding, using and managing environments for a range of purposes.

Week 13: Where to?: The future prospects for understanding and responding to global change, course wrap up and exam essay preparation. The future prospects for understanding and responding to global change, course wrap up and exam preparation.
